notes.meaning: Paul opens his letter alongside Silas and Timothy to the young church in Thessalonica. He does not use his formal title of apostle because he already shares a close and warm bond with them. They belong safely to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who give them grace, which is God's free favor, and his deep peace.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church teaching noted that Paul left out his title because these believers were brand new converts, and being described as in God showed the highest possible honor for a small local gathering.

notes.meaning: The missionary team constantly thanks God whenever they pray for all the believers in Thessalonica. They give God the credit for everything good taking place in the church, rather than praising human effort. Remembering fellow Christians regularly in prayer helps keep believers bound together in love.

Paul remembers three great gifts at work in the Thessalonians: faith, love, and hope. True faith is never lazy but produces good works, real love labors hard to care for others, and hope in Jesus gives steady endurance through trials. God our Father sees and delights in these living fruits of grace.

Paul calls the Thessalonians dear family who are loved by God, and he assures them that God has chosen them. He does not know this by reading secret heavenly records, but by seeing the unmistakable spiritual fruit in their lives. Knowing that God loves and chooses his people brings deep comfort.

differ.view: Election is God's eternal, unconditional choice of specific individuals to receive salvation and everlasting life, based solely on his sovereign grace and not on human merit.

Election is conditional on faith in Christ, and here it refers to God choosing and inviting the Gentiles into the blessings of the church rather than an unconditional decree choosing individuals to eternal glory.
Election primarily describes being admitted into the outward privileges and gifts of the Christian church in this present life, without guaranteeing a person's final salvation.
A person becomes a candidate for heaven at conversion, but is fully elected when cleansed and sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: The good news about Jesus did not reach the Thessalonians as mere human speech or clever talk. The Holy Spirit made the message powerful, stirring deep conviction in their hearts that it was true. At the same time, the missionaries backed up their words by living holy, selfless lives among them.

The believers followed the example of the apostles and of the Lord Jesus himself by welcoming the gospel message. Even though turning to Christ brought them painful persecution, the Holy Spirit gave them supernatural joy. Bearing hardship with spiritual joy is a sure sign of genuine faith.

Their steady courage made the Thessalonian church an example for other believers across Greece to follow. Even though they were brand new to the faith, their loyalty under fire gave strength to older churches. A faithful response to suffering can inspire and guide many other Christians.

The message of the Lord echoed outward from Thessalonica like the clear blast of a trumpet. Christian merchants and travelers spread the story of their faith through Greece and beyond. Their lives were such powerful testimonies that Paul had no need to tell others what God had done there.

People everywhere were telling the story of the warm welcome the Thessalonians gave the preachers. These former pagans had turned completely away from dead idols to serve the one true and living God. Genuine conversion always means turning away from false gods to devote your life to the Lord.

Believers now wait with patient hope for God's Son to return from heaven. God raised Jesus from the dead as proof of his victory, and Jesus rescues his people from the coming wrath, which is God's righteous judgment against sin. Looking forward to Christ's return gives Christians comfort and courage today.

differ.view: Deliverance from the coming wrath means Christ will remove the church before the terrible period of the Great Tribulation by catching up believers in a pre-tribulation rapture.
The wrath to come refers to God's final judgment and eternal punishment on the wicked at the Last Day, from which Jesus's death on the cross has rescued his people.
